answer:
Economics is the domain where the majority of authors tend to be male for both original and replication studies.

Executed analysis (unweighted, row-level; one row = one original × replication-lab pair; male-majority = ratio > 0.5):

| discipline | n | mean_male_o | mean_male_r | %rows>0.5 o | %rows>0.5 r | %both>0.5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cognitive | 241 | 0.77 | 0.51 | 75.9% | 52.7% | 41.1% |
| Economics | 18 | 0.87 | 0.84 | 77.8% | 72.2% | 55.6% |
| Social | 668 | 0.73 | 0.51 | 56.6% | 53.1% | 30.1% |

All three disciplines technically exceed 0.5 on both means, but only Economics shows a clear male majority in BOTH study types: original mean 0.87 and replication mean 0.84, with ~78% and ~72% of rows male-majority respectively. Social and Cognitive have strong male majorities in originals (0.73/0.77) but replication means of only ~0.51 — essentially at the coin-flip boundary, not a male majority tendency.

Sensitivity checks (both confirm the ranking):
1) Author-count-weighted means: Cognitive 0.802/0.530, Economics 0.875/0.814, Social 0.729/0.540.
2) Original-study-deduped mean(o): Cognitive 0.711, Economics 0.870, Social 0.658.

Caveats: Economics is a small cell (n=18 rows, 18 original studies, all from the 'ee'/Experimental Economics project), so its means are noisier; Social's replication mean (0.5055) is borderline and could flip with minor data changes. The second CSV (replication success data) has no gender or discipline fields and was not used.

Final hypothesis (concise, data-grounded):
"In Experimental Economics, the majority of authors tend to be male in both original and replication studies — the mean fraction of male authors is 0.87 for originals and 0.84 for replications (about 78% and 72% of studies are male-majority), far above the ~0.51 replication-side means seen in Social and Cognitive psychology, where male majorities appear mainly in the original studies. Caveat: Economics comprises only 18 original×replication pairs, so the estimate has higher uncertainty."

payload.workflow: Loaded the study-level CSV (927 rows; 0 missing in discipline/authors_male.o/authors_male.r; all ratios in [0,1]); grouped by discipline (Social 668, Cognitive 241, Economics 18) and computed unweighted row-level mean male-author ratios, % of rows with ratio > 0.5 (o, r, and both); ran two sensitivity checks (author-count-weighted means; original-study-deduped mean for .o). Economics showed the only clear male majority in both study types under all measures.
